{{Short description|Topic in mathematical analysis}}
In [[mathematical analysis|analysis]], a branch of mathematics, '''Hilbert's inequality''' states that

: <math>
\left|\sum_{r\neq s}\dfrac{u_{r}\overline{u_{s}}}{r-s}\right|\le\pi\displaystyle\sum_{r}|u_{r}|^2.
</math>

for any sequence {{math|''u''<sub>1</sub>,''u''<sub>2</sub>,...}} of complex numbers. It was first demonstrated by [[David Hilbert]] with the constant {{math|2{{pi}}}} instead of {{math|{{pi}}}}; the sharp constant was found by [[Issai Schur]]. It implies that the [[Hilbert transform#Discrete Hilbert transform|discrete Hilbert transform]] is a [[bounded operator]] in {{math|''ℓ''<sub>2</sub>}}.

==Formulation==

Let {{math|(''u''<sub>''m''</sub>)}} be a sequence of complex numbers. If the sequence is infinite, assume that it is square-summable:

:<math> \sum_m |u_m|^2 < \infty </math>

Hilbert's inequality (see {{harvtxt|Steele|2004}}) asserts that

: <math>
\left|\sum_{r\neq s}\dfrac{u_{r}\overline{u_{s}}}{r-s}\right|\le\pi\displaystyle\sum_{r}|u_{r}|^2.
</math>

==Extensions==

In 1973, [[#MV|Montgomery & Vaughan]] reported several generalizations of Hilbert's inequality, considering the bilinear forms

: <math> \sum_{r\neq s}u_r\overline u_s\csc\pi(x_r-x_s) </math>

and

: <math>\sum_{r\neq s}\dfrac{u_r\overline u_s}{\lambda_r-\lambda_s},</math>

where {{math|''x''<sub>1</sub>,''x''<sub>2</sub>,...,''x''<sub>''m''</sub>}} are distinct real numbers modulo&nbsp;1 (i.e. they belong to distinct classes in the [[quotient group]] {{math|'''R'''/'''Z'''}}) and {{math|''&lambda;''<sub>1</sub>,...,''&lambda;''<sub>''m''</sub>}} are distinct real numbers. [[#MV|Montgomery & Vaughan]]'s generalizations of Hilbert's inequality are then given by

: <math>
\left|\sum_{r\neq s} u_r \overline{u_s}\csc\pi(x_r-x_s)\right|\le\delta^{-1}\sum_r |u_r|^2.
</math>

and

: <math>
\left|\sum_{r\neq s}\dfrac{u_r\overline{u_s}}{\lambda_r-\lambda_s}\right|\le\pi\tau^{-1} \sum_r |u_r|^2.
</math>

where

:<math>\delta={\min_{r,s}}{}_{+}\|x_{r}-x_{s}\|, \quad \tau=\min_{r,s}{}_{+}\|\lambda_r-\lambda_s\|, </math>

:<math>\|s\|= \min_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}|s-m|</math>

is the distance from {{math|''s''}} to the nearest [[integer]], and {{math|min<sub>+</sub>}} denotes the smallest positive value. Moreover, if

:<math>0<\delta_r \le {\min_s}{}_{+}\|x_r-x_s\| \quad \text{and} \quad 0<\tau_{r}\le {\min_{s}}{}_{+}\|\lambda_r-\lambda_s\|,</math>

then the following inequalities hold:

: <math>
\left|\sum_{r\neq s} u_r\overline{u_s}\csc\pi(x_r-x_s)\right|\le\dfrac{3}{2} \sum_r |u_r|^2 \delta_r^{-1}.
</math>

and

: <math>\left|\sum_{r\neq s}\dfrac{u_r \overline{u_s}}{\lambda_r-\lambda_s}\right|\le \dfrac{3}{2} \pi \sum_r |u_r|^2\tau_r^{-1}.
</math>
